title: Technical deep dive - Llama/Mistral/Qwen MoE routing & RoPE scaling
summary: Deep technical session focused on model-architecture specific tuning for production inference. Covered tradeoffs of batching and KV cache strategies, quantization options, and special considerations for Llama/Mistral/Qwen and MoE models. Discussed RoPE scaling impacts on long contexts and VPC/on-prem latency constraints. Agreed next steps: run targeted benchmarks, share benchmark spreadsheet and security docs, and scope a pilot for Dedicated capacity with MoE cost analysis.
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~75 minutes
- Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood Infra), Sara (Atlas ML), Ethan (Atlas ML), Priya (Atlas Security), John (Atlas SRE)

Summary (auto):
- High-level: Atlas wants to understand fine-grained perf tradeoffs when serving Llama-family and Mistral/Qwen models, plus MoE routing overhead and RoPE scaling for longer contexts.
- Focus on: KV cache strategy, batching (dynamic vs continuous), 4-bit quantization behavior, on-prem networking and KMS, and gating costs for MoE.

----- Transcript -----
00:00 Alex: okay hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Alex from Redwood. we've got Maya and Diego from my side, and I think we have Sara, Ethan, Priya and John from Atlas, is that right?
00:06 Sara: yeah that's right, hey, uh thanks for setting this up. we wanted a deep dive — we have an evaluation window and need to decide model families and infra.
00:11 Maya: awesome, high level agenda — runtime perf, kv cache, batching, quant, and then model-specific notes for Llama, Mistral, Qwen and MoE routing / RoPE. we'll try to keep it pragmatic.
00:19 Ethan: good, especially interested in MoE. our research lead thinks MoE could give 2-3x throughput but we're worried about gating and routing overhead.
00:26 Diego: yes, MoE is tricky in serving because the router logic and expert parameter sharding add tail costs and memory pressure.
00:31 John: also want to be sure VPC/on-prem network egress doesn't blow latency SLOs for our interactive product.
00:36 Maya: makes sense. starting with KV cache: Atlas has a lot of multi-turn chat, so prefix caching matters. we often recommend prefix/KV caching per-conversation and shared prefix caches for common system prompts.
00:46 Ethan: quick Q — is the KV cache single copy per model replica or sharded across GPUs?
00:51 Diego: by default in Redwood Dedicated we keep KV cache per replica and manage cache warming during routing. for large-context (8k+), we use sliced KV so each GPU holds local shards of KV to avoid OOM. it's not perfectly single-copy unless you configure cross-replica sharding.
01:03 Maya: practical tip — for Llama and Mistral, kv cache grows linearly with context tokens, but Mistral's optimized attention sometimes uses less memory due to fused kernels; results vary by sequence distribution.
01:14 Ethan: hmm ok. what about prefix dedupe / substring cache? we have a bunch of identical system prompts.
01:19 Alex: we support prefix dedupe — you can precompute and store KV for those system prompts and reuse them, that reduces per-request token generation by the length of the prefix and improves latency. but note: dedupe only helps if the model variant and quantization match exactly.
01:30 Sara: good to know. next on batching — we've read about continuous batching vs fixed micro-batches. what's recommended for interactive low-latency?
01:37 Maya: for interactive, continuous (or streaming-aware) batching with small max batch sizes gives best latency while still getting batching wins. e.g., 4-8 token-level micro-batching with max wait 10-15ms. continuous batching yields better tail latency than waiting fixed 50-100ms windows.
01:49 John: do you expose parameters to tune max batch size and wait time?
01:52 Diego: yes, those are runtime knobs in the serving config. we also auto-suggest based on observed qps and sequence length histograms.
01:58 Ethan: any special handling for Mistral / Qwen? their memory accesses differ right?
02:02 Maya: Mistral tends to be more memory friendly at equivalent params due to dense layer fusions, so it tolerates slightly larger batches. Qwen sometimes benefits from bigger batch sizes but shows more variance; you should profile per model.
02:12 Alex: now quantization — we support PTQ 8-bit and 4-bit modes. the 4-bit route has two flavors: outlier-aware asymmetric PTQ and a more aggressive 4-bit QAT path.
02:21 Ethan: what accuracy hit do you see on Llama-2 13B for 4-bit PTQ?
02:24 Maya: typically 0.5-1.5% relative on standard evals for well-calibrated outlier-aware 4-bit. but results vary; Mistral sometimes tolerates 4-bit even better, Qwen might lose slightly more on rare tokens. we recommend an eval harness for your prompts.
02:38 Sara: operationally, does quantization change KV cache layout?
02:41 Diego: yes, quantized KV uses compressed representations; it reduces memory and bandwidth but increases CPU/GPU dequant overhead per token. for some kernels that are memory-bound, quantization still yields net perf wins; for compute-bound kernels, the dequant overhead can offset gains.
02:55 Ethan: about MoE routing — what are the main hidden costs?
02:58 Maya: two big costs: router compute and expert scatter/gather. router is relatively cheap per token, but gating decisions cause communication overhead when experts are sharded across devices. if you have per-expert replicas on different GPUs, you pay network all-to-all for expert activations.
03:12 Alex: practical guidance — to get MoE throughput gains you need to ensure expert locality: colocate or pin experts so the majority of selected experts are local to the device or use a hybrid sharding strategy. otherwise the extra all-to-all can wipe out advantages.
03:26 Ethan: do you have measured numbers?
03:28 Diego: rough numbers from our lab: MoE with local experts yields up to 2.5-3x throughput vs dense at similar FLOPs. with cross-device expert scatter it drops to ~1.1-1.4x and tail latency increases 30-60%.
03:39 Sara: and memory-wise? MoE parameter count is bigger but active memory per token is similar?
03:44 Maya: yes, model size is larger but only the activated experts are used per token; still you need memory for routing buffers and for worst-case hotspots when many tokens pick same expert.
03:54 Ethan: routing randomness — do you throttle or use capacity factors?
03:56 Maya: we use capacity factors and secondary experts with a routing fallback. that helps avoid hotspots but increases average expert invocations slightly. tradeoff your throughput vs deterministic latency.
04:07 Priya: security question — if we run MoE on Dedicated in our VPC, does routing cross the control plane or stay within customer network?
04:13 Diego: all data plane traffic stays within the customer VPC for Redwood Private / Dedicated. control plane orchestration signals are minimal and can be routed via our private control plane or customer-hosted control plane for air-gapped installs. we support KMS/HSM for keys and audit logs for gating decisions too.
04:27 John: network latency: what's typical extra ms if customer on-prem has a front-end in their VPC and model on dedicated cluster in same region?
04:33 Alex: for colocated within same AZ and private network, we see sub-ms to low ms networking; typical 1-5ms added. cross-AZ or cross-region will add tens of ms. for interactive SLOs you want to keep model and frontend same AZ when possible.
04:45 Sara: RoPE — our product sometimes needs 32k context for summarization. we've read that RoPE scaling can break with very long contexts. what's Redwood's experience?
04:53 Maya: RoPE (rotary positional embeddings) scaling is model-dependent. standard RoPE parameters assume a fixed base frequency; scaling up context naively can lead to phase mismatch. two approaches: 1) RoPE remapping/rescaling (decay or linear scaling) or 2) position interpolation techniques. Llama-family variants often need explicit RoPE re-scaling for >16k. Mistral and Qwen may have different nominal RoPE bases.
05:12 Ethan: does re-scaling require model surgery / re-embedding?
05:15 Maya: sometimes yes — you can rescale rotary freq at runtime by applying a multiplier to sin/cos positions which helps extend context without re-training, but it's not perfect and can degrade long-coherence for very far tokens. some teams retrain or finetune with longer RoPE ranges.
05:27 Alex: we can run controlled benchmarks — e.g., 8k->32k sequences and measure perplexity and decoding divergence, to recommend either runtime rescale or finetune path.
05:35 Sara: great. any differences in tooling for Llama vs Qwen?
05:38 Maya: Llama forks often have community tooling that supports RoPE rescale scripts; Qwen and Mistral sometimes ship different position encodings or slightly different rotary freq defaults, so our model onboarding tests include a RoPE sensitivity suite.
05:49 Ethan: okay, practical serving questions — what about batching + kv for streaming tokens? we want minimal tail latency for first token and maintain throughput for later tokens.
05:58 Diego: that's the classic trade. we prioritize first-token latency with fast-path for small batches and warm persistent sessions for multi-turn RL. streaming incremental generation can use prefix cache aggressively: warm the prefix and then generate tokens with very small micro-batches. also prefetch kernels so GPU warmup is minimized.
06:14 Alex: also consider per-route model variants: keep a low-latency quantized variant for quick replies and a high-quality variant for longer completions or high-cost flows. Redwood's routing can do per-customer route policies with automatic fallback.
06:25 Priya: audit question — do you log routing decisions (which expert was used) to audit logs? data privacy concerns.
06:30 Diego: we can log routing metadata (expert ids, timing) as audit logs without including raw token content. for sensitive workflows you can opt-out or encrypt logs with customer KMS.
06:40 Sara: we want to run our own benchmarks; what artifacts will you share?
06:43 Alex: we'll share a benchmark spreadsheet with per-model perf numbers, kernel-level breakdowns (memory vs compute), and recommended config knobs: batch size ranges, wait times, cache policies, and quant settings.
06:55 Ethan: and can you run a pilot with our sample prompts and MoE layout? we'd like to test 2 expert configurations and local vs shuffled expert sharding.
07:03 Maya: yes, we can schedule bench runs — we'll need a sample prompt set, target throughput SLO and cost constraints. we can then run Dedicated pilot with pinned expert colocation.
07:11 Sara: timeline?
07:12 Alex: we can turn around initial numbers in 7-10 business days assuming you provide prompts and access for a short test account.
07:17 Priya: security pack — send SOC2 and KMS integration docs.
07:20 Diego: will do, plus on-prem install notes for air-gapped setup.
07:24 Ethan: one last item: rope and tokenization mismatch — sometimes our tokenization and model tokenizer diverge; does that affect RoPE rescale?
07:29 Maya: tokenization mismatches affect input length but not RoPE math directly; however differing tokenization can change effective sequence length and thereby impact memory/kv planning. recommend using the exact tokenizer shipped with model for accurate benchmarks.
07:40 Alex: great — recap and next steps in a minute.
07:42 Sara: quick interrupt, there's a point about MoE gating that I didn't get: does Redwood support top-k gating or noisy-top-k?
07:47 Maya: we support noisy-top-k and capacity-factor gating in our MoE runtime. we also instrument per-token gate entropy to detect degenerate routing.
07:54 Sara: ok thanks.
07:56 Alex: recap of next steps and action items.

----- End Transcript -----
